text.en: Open your kitchen shelf and you will find turmeric, cumin, cloves and more. For many Indian families these spices are also home remedies. In this chapter a grandmother writes a letter to her grandchildren and shares what she learnt from her own grandmother. Let us read her advice and learn to use it safely.

A spice is any seed, fruit, root, bark, leaf or other part of a plant used to give taste and colour to food. The book lists ten spices: turmeric, fenugreek, cumin seeds, asafoetida, cinnamon, clove, ginger, black pepper, fennel seeds and cardamom. Find out their names in your language. Spices can also be used for things other than cooking, which is what the letter explains.
The letter is from Daadi, a grandmother, to her grandchildren Vikram and Vaibhavi. She is happy that they are better now and that the natural cures she shared helped. She asks them to try to remember these cures and share them with friends. She learnt them as a child from her own grandmother, who found home remedies in the kitchen for most of the common illnesses that come with the weather. So natural cures are passed from one generation to another.
Haldi, or turmeric, helps in improving our energy level and digestion, and in reducing body pain. Methi, or fenugreek, helps keep sugar level and body weight in control when the seeds are soaked overnight and the water is drunk in the morning. Jeera, or cumin, soaked overnight can improve digestion and help with sleeplessness. Heeng, or asafoetida, was put as water on the babies' tummies to give relief from gas, and it can also help with cough and cold.
Dalchini (cinnamon) and laung (clove) give relief in toothache until we can consult a dentist. Adrak (ginger) helps in cough and cold and gives relief from pain. It has been used in cooking for more than four thousand years. Kali mirch (black pepper) helps digestion and gives relief from body pain. Saunf (fennel) and ajwain (carom) are served at the end of a meal because they help digestion. Elaichi (cardamom) helps digestion and breathing troubles and cures bad breath.
Daadi ends with an important piece of advice: go into the kitchen, identify the herbs and spices, and remember that you must consult an elder before you use them. Natural remedies can support small, common troubles, but they do not replace a doctor. For serious or lasting illness we must see a doctor. Notice that fennel seeds are named for digestion, not for body pain. Reading carefully is how you answer questions about this letter.
Spices come from different parts of plants. Turmeric is a root, cinnamon is bark, clove is a flower bud, black pepper and cardamom are fruits or seeds, and fenugreek, cumin and fennel are seeds. Each spice has a colour, a texture and a taste. Use words like rough, soft, silky for texture and bitter, sweet, sour, salty or spicy for taste. Describing a spice with these words is the speaking task: introduce yourself as a spice and say your name, part of the plant, colour, texture, taste and benefits.
Modal verbs, or helping verbs, show things like ability, advice and necessity. In the letter: may share, should try, can help, must consult, need to soak and used to put. May gives a suggestion or possibility. Should gives advice. Can shows ability. Must shows compulsion. Need to shows necessity. Used to shows a past habit. Example dialogue: Anand had fever, so he should take rest. He must take rest or he will fall ill again. He can take grandmother's natural cures. We need to remember how effective they are.
Tulsi, or holy basil, is called the Queen of Herbs. It is said to have been first found in north central India and now grows almost everywhere. It helps decrease glucose and cholesterol levels, improves blood pressure and is used for breathing and digestion trouble. It has anti-bacterial properties and is used in herbal hand sanitisers, mouth washes and toothpaste. Tulsi leaves can be washed and eaten raw or added to tea, and tulsi tea helps with stress. A recipe uses steps: first take, then grate, mix, warm, and have it three to four times a day. For the ginger and honey cough remedy the steps include grating fresh ginger, taking its juice and mixing with honey. Riddles can help you guess spices, for example the spice that comes from under the ground, has been used for thousands of years and cures a cold is ginger.

problem.en: Match the helping verb with its function: may, should, can, must, need to, used to.

text.en: Think of what each word expresses.

why.en: May suggests possibility; should gives advice.

text.en: Can is ability; must is compulsion; need to is necessity; used to is past habit.

why.en: Each modal has a different job.

problem.en: Complete: Anand had fever last week. He ____ take good rest.

text.en: The sentence gives advice.
The sentence is: He should take good rest.

prompt.en: Explain how Daadi's letter shows that natural cures pass from generation to generation, and what safety advice she gave.

requiredIdeas.en: Daadi learnt cures from her grandmother and shares them with her grandchildren.
She asks them to remember and share them.
She lists spices such as turmeric, fenugreek and ginger and their uses.
She says to consult an elder before use.

points.en: Spices are plant parts used for taste and colour.
Daadi explains how turmeric, fenugreek, cumin, ginger, pepper, fennel and cardamom help.
Natural cures are passed from one generation to the next.
Always consult an elder or doctor before using any remedy.
Modal verbs show advice, ability, necessity and habit.
Tulsi is the Queen of Herbs.
